meta.tagline: Imperial elegance, coffeehouse philosophy and a slice of Sachertorte

pills: One of the world's most livable cities

overview.title: Welcome to Vienna
overview.intro: Vienna neither locked its old splendour in a museum nor put it up for sale; it simply kept living in it. Trams glide past palaces, students snap up the standing tickets at the opera, and a retiree reading the paper in a marble coffeehouse sits for hours without anyone bringing the bill. This city smiles politely at hurry: 'Sit down, have a Melange, the world can wait.' Do the same — Vienna only opens up once you slow down.

local_word.definition: Vienna's untranslatable humour: half mocking, half affectionate, always an elegant art of the well-placed jab. The waiter's deadpan joke is Schmäh; the day you get it, you've become Viennese.

rules.title: In a coffeehouse, the table is yours
rules.description: Order one coffee and sit for hours: newspapers, conversation, doing nothing at all — all perfectly legitimate. The waiter (Herr Ober) may seem aloof; that's not rudeness, it's a centuries-old role. The bill never comes unless you ask.

rules.title: Standing tickets at the opera are cheap
rules.description: The State Opera sells standing places (Stehplätze) for a few euros, at the box office shortly before the performance. That's the Viennese way to enter the world's best stage on a student budget.

rules.title: Don't look for a ticket gate — but don't ride without one
rules.description: The U-Bahn has no turnstiles; the system runs on trust, but inspectors are plain-clothed and unforgiving. Buy a weekly or 72-hour pass on day one and explore with peace of mind.

tip.label: The Viennese philosophy
tip.text: The Viennese have two speeds: slow and slower. Asking the time in a coffeehouse, clapping too early at a concert and standing on the left of an escalator — the three local sins. Everything else is forgiven.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Vienna's public transport is the city's pride: punctual, clean and running through the night. Don't even think about a car.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The CAT express reaches Wien Mitte in 16 minutes; the S7 commuter train does it slightly slower for half the price. Taxis have a flat rate, but with trains this comfortable they're unnecessary.

items.title: U-Bahn — the five-colour backbone
items.description: Five lines weave the city together and run 24 hours on weekend nights. The 24/48/72-hour passes and the weekly card are tourist-friendly; validate your ticket on first boarding.

items.title: Ring tour by tram
items.description: Trams 1 and 2 carry you past the palaces of the Ringstrasse for the price of a normal ticket: skip the tourist bus, take a window seat.

items.title: WienMobil bikes
items.description: Shared bikes are a joy along the canal and out to the Prater; bike lanes are wide and drivers respectful. Pedalling the Danube Island is the city's best summer escape.

items.title: The 1st district on foot
items.description: Everything inside the Ring is walkable end to end: cathedral, palace and coffeehouses are always ten minutes apart. Comfortable shoes are all the cobblestones ask for.

callout.label: Tram tip
callout.text: Do the Ring tour in late afternoon: as the Opera, Parliament and Rathaus light up at golden hour, the window of tram 2 becomes the city's cheapest palace box.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Vienna the district (Bezirk) number is as much identity as address: 1st means grandeur, 7th means cool, 2nd means green.

local_word.definition: Each of Vienna's 23 administrative districts; addresses are spoken by number. Saying 'I live in the Siebter' (the 7th) tells a Viennese a whole paragraph about you.

items.name: Innere Stadt (1st Bezirk)
items.description: The museum-city inside the Ring: cathedral, palace and coffeehouses right outside your door. Prices are at imperial levels, the streets surprisingly calm at night — the classic for a first visit.

items.name: Neubau (7th Bezirk)
items.description: The design-and-café quarter behind the MuseumsQuartier: independent boutiques, third-wave coffee, young Vienna. Walking distance to the centre, the soul of a neighbourhood.

items.name: Leopoldstadt (2nd Bezirk)
items.description: The district of the Prater and the Danube Canal: a giant park, the Ferris wheel, bars along the water. The area around the Karmeliter market is young and lively; prices friendlier than the centre.

items.name: Josefstadt (8th Bezirk)
items.description: Vienna's smallest district: theatres, antique dealers, quiet Biedermeier streets. Low on tourists, high on coffeehouses — for those after calm elegance.

items.name: Wieden (4th Bezirk)
items.description: Neighbour to the Naschmarkt and Karlsplatz: walk to the market, walk to the opera, dine at a neighbourhood tavern in the evening. The address where central comfort meets neighbourhood prices.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Vienna is on stage in all four seasons: spring is a garden, summer a film, autumn a wine, winter a ball.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Garden Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Blooming parks, full cafés
items.description: The gardens of Schönbrunn and Belvedere burst into flower, the Naschmarkt stalls overflow, coffeehouse tables spill onto the pavements. The city is at its most photogenic and most balanced.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: In late May the Wiener Festwochen begins: the city turns into a stage, and the opening concert on Rathausplatz is free.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Open-Air Season
items.subtitle: Summer · Film festival, canal beaches
items.description: Free concert films on a giant screen at Rathausplatz with world-food stands in front; the Danube Island and the canal 'beaches' are the city's summer resort. Hotels are relatively calm; some institutions take holidays.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: The Film Festival evening formula: snacks from the Naschmarkt, a blanket on Rathausplatz, opera on the big screen — total cost close to zero.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Harvest and Sturm
items.subtitle: Autumn · Heuriger season, golden parks
items.description: The harvest begins in the city's own vineyards; half-fermented Sturm is poured at the heurigers and the smell of roast chestnuts drifts through the streets. By mid-November the Christmas markets switch their lights on early.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: Walk from Kahlenberg down through the vineyards to Nussdorf and sit down at a heuriger on the way: Sturm + home cooking + city views. That is Viennese autumn in one afternoon.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Balls and Markets
items.subtitle: Winter · Christmas markets, ball season, the New Year waltz
items.description: In December the square before the Rathaus becomes a sea of light; in January and February hundreds of balls are held — some sell tickets to visitors. On January 1st the whole city watches the New Year's Concert on screens.

callout.label: December note
callout.text: Christmas markets are packed on weekends; drink your Punsch on a weekday evening, and you can keep the mug deposit as a souvenir.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Viennese cuisine is the empire's inheritance: Hungarian goulash, Czech dumplings, Italian coffee — all ennobled in this city.

local_word.definition: Vienna's national coffee: half espresso, half milk foam — the cappuccino's elegant cousin. It arrives on a tray with a glass of water; that water is coffeehouse language for 'stay as long as you like'.

items.name: Wiener Schnitzel — the real one is veal
items.description: A schnitzel overflowing the plate, paper-thin, fried in butter: potato salad on the side, lemon on top. Go where it says 'vom Kalb' (veal); everything else is imitation.
items.tag: At a classic tavern · make it vom Kalb

items.name: The coffeehouse ritual — Melange + Sachertorte
items.description: Marble tables, newspapers, a waiter in no hurry: the coffeehouse is not a venue but a way of life. Don't order your Sachertorte without Schlag — the cream is part of the balance.
items.tag: In a historic coffeehouse · never rushed

items.name: The Würstelstand late-night classic
items.description: Sausage stands are Vienna's midnight kitchen: order the cheese-filled Käsekrainer with bread and sweet mustard. Opera-goers in black tie and night-shift workers share the same counter — the city's most democratic table.

items.name: Tafelspitz — the emperor's pot
items.description: Boiled beef with bone marrow, apple-horseradish and chive sauce: the dish Emperor Franz Joseph ate every day. It looks heavy, it eats elegantly.

items.name: A heuriger evening
items.description: Wine taverns in the city's own vineyards: young wine, cold platters from the buffet, long wooden tables. A pine branch over the door means they're open — Vienna in its village clothes.
items.tag: At a vineyard tavern · open if the pine branch is out

items.name: A Naschmarkt crawl
items.description: The city's century-old market: pickle vendors, meze counters and world kitchens side by side. On Saturdays a flea market joins in; grazing your way through is entirely allowed.
items.tag: Saturday morning · graze as you go

callout.label: The coffeehouse rule
callout.text: Skip the famous coffeehouse with the queue and pick the quiet one around the corner: same Melange, same marble, more Schmäh. In Vienna the best coffeehouse is the one where you can get a seat.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the palaces; these six are Vienna's backstage.

items.name: Prunksaal — National Library
items.description: The baroque library hall inside the Hofburg: 200,000 leather-bound volumes, a frescoed dome, imperial globes. Less famous than the opera, with a shorter queue — Viennese splendour in distilled form.

items.name: Kirche am Steinhof
items.description: Otto Wagner's golden-domed church on a hilltop, standing inside hospital grounds — the city's least-known masterpiece. It opens on Sunday afternoons; plan around that.

items.rarity: A city of the dead, a park for the living
items.name: Zentralfriedhof
items.description: The vast cemetery where Beethoven, Schubert and the Strausses rest is also a park where deer wander: take tram 71 out and walk inside it for hours. Not mournful — serene.

items.rarity: Through the vineyards into the city
items.name: The Kahlenberg to Nussdorf walk
items.description: Take the bus to the top, then descend towards the city through the vines: the Danube, the domes and the vineyards in one frame. The walk ends at a heuriger's door — not a coincidence, a tradition.

items.name: Palmenhaus and Schmetterlinghaus
items.description: The glass palace at the edge of the Burggarten: one wing a tropical butterfly house, the other a brasserie under palm trees. The greenest way to drink coffee in a palace garden.

items.name: Servitenviertel
items.description: Bistros and bookshops gathered around a church square in the 9th Bezirk: next door to the Freud Museum, far from the tourists. The city's sweetest detour for an afternoon coffee.

callout.label: Museum tip
callout.text: On Thursday evenings you can sit in the café under the dome of the Kunsthistorisches Museum with live music: two floors above the Bruegels, a Melange amid the marble — a museum ticket is the cheapest ball in town.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Vienna is an honest city; its traps wear wigs and costumes, which makes them easy to spot.

items.name: Costumed 'Mozart concert' sellers
items.description: The concerts hawked by bewigged sellers around the cathedral follow one formula: mediocre orchestra plus inflated price. Mozart would have laughed at the whole business.
items.instead: Get the real thing for the same money: student or standing tickets at the Musikverein or Konzerthaus, or the State Opera's few-euro Stehplatz.

items.name: A fiaker ride without agreeing terms
items.description: Carriage tours have official tariffs, but if duration and route aren't agreed, a short ride can end with a long bill.
items.instead: Confirm the tariff and duration before boarding; or do the same route on tram 2, passing the very same palaces.

items.name: Losing an hour in one coffeehouse queue
items.description: Waiting 45 minutes outside the one or two coffeehouses social media has polished is an injustice to the city's two hundred others.
items.instead: When you see a queue, walk two streets on: in Vienna every neighbourhood has a marble-tabled, chandeliered, quiet coffeehouse of its own.

items.name: The 'Viennese menu' at the cathedral's feet
items.description: The picture menus around Stephansplatz sell lukewarm schnitzel at tourist prices.
items.instead: Go two streets deeper, or pick the neighbourhood taverns (Beisl) of the 4th and 7th Bezirk: the same schnitzel, half the price, the real thing.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Stay away from anyone who puts on a costume to sell you something in Vienna; in this city, real grandeur wears no uniform — it sits in a coffeehouse reading the paper.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A Vienna digest, from empire to coffeehouse

steps.title: The cathedral and morning streets
steps.description: See the tiled roof of the Stephansdom in morning light; walk the imperial shopfronts of Graben and Kohlmarkt while they're still empty.

steps.title: Hofburg + Prunksaal
steps.description: Pass through the palace courtyards, then stand quietly under the dome of the baroque library: Vienna's most concentrated dose of beauty.

steps.title: Lunch at the Naschmarkt
steps.description: Graze stall by stall, then a sit-down break at a market tavern; if it's Saturday, the flea market is a bonus.

steps.title: Belvedere — Klimt's Kiss
steps.description: Stand before The Kiss in the Upper Belvedere, then look out over the city from the gardens; your art quota is full for the day.

steps.title: The Ring tour by tram
steps.description: From the window of tram 2, the parade of Opera, Parliament and Rathaus: at golden hour the palaces turn to light.

steps.title: Coffeehouse + a late-night close
steps.description: A long coffeehouse sit with Melange and Sachertorte; a Käsekrainer from a Würstelstand on the way home — an imperial day ends with a sausage.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The imperial classics
steps.description: The one-day flow above: cathedral, Hofburg, Naschmarkt, Belvedere, the Ring.

steps.title: Schönbrunn and the museums
steps.description: Early morning at Schönbrunn (climb to the Gloriette, get lost in the maze), afternoon at the Kunsthistorisches or the MuseumsQuartier; evening in the 7th Bezirk for a Beisl dinner and a bar crawl.

steps.title: Vineyards and farewell
steps.description: The vineyard walk from Kahlenberg, a heuriger lunch; on the way back, visit Beethoven at the Zentralfriedhof, and in the evening a standing ticket at the State Opera or the Musikverein — farewell music is mandatory.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Viennese German is polite and musical; these five carry you from the coffeehouse door to the ballroom.

items.meaning: The Austrian greeting: 'good day' — formal and valid everywhere
Thank you — upgraded by vielen Dank
Please / you're welcome / here you go — you'll hear it fifty times a day
Cheers! — no glass is raised without eye contact
'It's fine, no problem' — the official phrase of Viennese ease; also how you say keep the change

items.sub: Melange, a newspaper and a marble table — no rushing allowed
